name: Hydroxyzine (Vistaril, Atarax)
summary: Sedating antihistamine sometimes used as a non-benzodiazepine option for short-term anxiety, bedtime anxiety insomnia, or acute “take the edge off” agitation. Works fast, but can leave you groggy and has QT-prolongation risk in susceptible people.
description: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine that can calm anxiety and help with sleep when anxiety is driving the problem. It can kick in within 15–30 minutes by mouth, but the sedation can carry into the next morning. It’s not a benzo and doesn’t create the same dependence pattern, but it’s still a real sedative—mixing with alcohol or other downers can get dangerous. It also has a conditional QT-prolongation risk, so it’s not for everyone.
patient_summary: Hydroxyzine can be a quick, non-benzodiazepine way to calm anxiety or help you sleep when anxiety is the main issue. It works fast, but it can make you drowsy (sometimes into the next day), and it’s not a great fit if you’re older, have heart rhythm risk, or take other meds that prolong QT. No alcohol. No “let’s see how this feels” before driving.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Antiemetic; Histamine H1 Antagonist (First Generation); Piperazine Derivative

linked_conditions.context: Often used as a short-term or as-needed option for anxiety symptoms, especially when benzodiazepines are not preferred. It can be a temporary bridge while maintenance treatments (therapy, SSRIs/SNRIs) ramp up.
Sometimes used at bedtime when anxiety is the main driver of insomnia. The tradeoff is next-day grogginess, especially at higher doses or in people who metabolize it slowly.
May help mild-to-moderate anxiety-related agitation as a sedating PRN, but it is not a primary emergency tranquilizer and can impair cognition and coordination.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to hydroxyzine or any component of the formulation
Prolonged QT interval (oral hydroxyzine is contraindicated in patients with prolonged QT)
Early pregnancy (contraindicated based on animal reproduction data and labeling)
Oral formulation: hypersensitivity to cetirizine or levocetirizine
Injection: IV, subcutaneous, or intra-arterial administration (contraindicated; IM only)

efficacy_response.metric: Short-term symptom relief (anxiety tension and somatic arousal)
efficacy_response.patient_text: Hydroxyzine can take the edge off quickly for some people, especially when anxiety feels physical (tight chest, jittery, wired-but-tired). It’s best thought of as a short-term symptom-relief tool—not a long-term anxiety plan.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Product labeling and clinical use patterns

pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: ~2 hours (oral serum peak reported in adult data)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: ~20 hours in adults (can be longer in older adults and hepatic dysfunction)
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Sedation and symptom effects can vary widely; next-day drowsiness is possible, especially after bedtime dosing
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic to multiple metabolites, including cetirizine (active)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine; active metabolite (cetirizine) is renally eliminated and may accumulate in kidney impairment
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken without regard to food

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Hydroxyzine is a sedating antihistamine that’s sometimes used in psychiatry as a non-benzodiazepine option for short-term anxiety relief, bedtime anxiety insomnia, or mild-to-moderate agitation when anxiety is the driver. It’s not a maintenance medication for chronic anxiety—but it can be a useful “bridge” while longer-term treatments start working.
items: {link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Anxiety symptom relief}: A short-term or as-needed way to reduce anxiety intensity
{link:condition:insomnia:Insomnia tied to anxiety}: Bedtime dosing when anxiety is keeping you awake
{link:condition:agitation:Anxiety-related agitation}: Calming effect for mild-to-moderate restlessness (not an emergency sedative)
off_label: Sleep initiation support when anxiety is the main trigger
PRN calming for situational anxiety when you want to avoid benzodiazepines

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Hydroxyzine experiences tend to fall into a few predictable buckets:

quotes: It didn’t feel like a benzo—more like my body finally unclenched.
My mind slowed down enough to stop spiraling.
It took the edge off without that ‘I don’t care about anything’ feeling.
I slept… but I paid for it the next morning.
It worked, but I woke up feeling heavy and foggy.
Great for bedtime anxiety. Bad idea before an early meeting.
items.note: Next-day drowsiness is common, especially with bedtime dosing, higher doses, or slower metabolism.

quotes: A little dizzy when I stood up too fast.
items.note: As a first-generation antihistamine, it can cause anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision), which hit older adults harder.

quotes: It calmed me, but I was not sharp.
I felt slower—safe at home, not great for driving.
My anxiety improved, but my productivity didn’t.
items.note: Cognitive slowing can happen, especially with morning and evening dosing.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Hydroxyzine tends to work quickly, but the sedation can last longer than you expect.
key_points: 15–30 minutes: You may start feeling calmer after an oral dose
~2 hours: Peak levels after oral dosing (often where sedation is strongest)
Overnight to next morning: Bedtime doses can cause morning grogginess
~20 hours: Average adult half-life (longer in older adults and liver impairment)
IM: Rapid onset when injected into a muscle (IM only; never IV)

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Hydroxyzine can be genuinely helpful for short-term anxiety relief—especially when anxiety is loud in the body (restless, tense, keyed-up). It’s not a “fix the anxiety disorder” medication. Think of it as a PRN calming tool or a bedtime anxiety helper, not a long-term plan.
sections.clinical_details: In real-world psychiatry use, hydroxyzine is often positioned as an alternative to benzodiazepines for situational anxiety or a bridge while maintenance therapy becomes effective. The tradeoff is sedation and anticholinergic side effects, and it carries QT-prolongation risk in susceptible patients.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Sedation + QT risk are the two big things people underestimate.
other: QT prolongation/torsades risk: Hydroxyzine has a conditional risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes in susceptible patients (especially with other QT-prolonging meds, electrolyte disturbances, kidney/liver impairment, bradycardia, or structural heart disease).
CNS depression: Drowsiness and dizziness can impair driving and operating machinery—sometimes into the next morning after bedtime dosing.
Older adults: Generally avoid due to strong anticholinergic burden (confusion, constipation, urinary retention, falls).
Pregnancy: Contraindicated in early pregnancy; neonatal withdrawal symptoms (including seizures) have been reported after chronic maternal use or large doses near term.
IM safety: IM only. IV, subcutaneous, and intra-arterial administration are contraindicated and can cause severe tissue injury and vascular complications.
patient_counseling: Treat your first dose like a ‘test dose’ on a low-demand day—this med can flatten you.
No alcohol. Mixing sedatives stacks the risk (oversedation, impaired coordination, accidents).
Avoid driving until you know your response—morning-after grogginess is a real thing.
Tell your clinician if you have fainting, palpitations, a known prolonged QT, or you take other QT-prolonging meds.
If you’re 65+, this is usually a ‘no’ because the anticholinergic side effects and fall risk are not worth it.
If you’re pregnant or might be pregnant, talk to your prescriber before taking it.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: drowsiness, dizziness, dry mouth, and cognitive slowing. The more you take (or the more sedating meds you stack), the more this turns into next-day fog and safety issues.
plain_language_list: Drowsiness / sedation (can persist into the next morning)

common.patient_note: This is the headline effect. It can help anxiety and sleep, but it can also make you feel ‘heavy,’ foggy, and uncoordinated. Bedtime dosing can spill into the next morning.
Especially noticeable when standing quickly or combining with other sedatives. Falls are a bigger risk in older adults.
Classic first-generation antihistamine effect. Hydration and sugar-free gum can help, but if you also get constipation or urinary retention, that’s a sign the anticholinergic burden is too high.
Some people feel slower or less sharp, especially with morning + evening dosing. If your job requires high-alert performance, this may be a bad fit.

serious: QT prolongation and torsades de pointes (rare): higher risk with existing QT prolongation, electrolyte abnormalities, bradycardia, structural heart disease, kidney/liver impairment, and other QT-prolonging medications.
Severe oversedation (especially with other CNS depressants): confusion, falls, accidents, and impaired breathing risk at high doses or when combined with sedatives.
Severe skin reactions (rare): acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) has been reported.
Neuropsychiatric effects (rare): hallucinations or involuntary movements have been reported; seizures have been reported at high doses.
IM administration injury (serious if incorrect route): tissue necrosis and vascular complications have been reported with inadvertent IV/intra-arterial/subcutaneous exposure.

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Hydroxyzine is a sedating, anticholinergic antihistamine. The biggest interaction problems are sedation stacking and QT risk stacking.

items.risk: Additive CNS depression: worse sedation, impaired judgment and coordination, higher accident risk, and potentially dangerous oversedation.

items.with: Other CNS depressants (opioids, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, muscle relaxants, sedating antihistamines, some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Sedation stacking: confusion, falls, driving impairment, and higher risk of dangerous oversedation.
items.action: Use the lowest effective doses, avoid combining when possible, and do not drive until you know the combined effect.

items.with: QT-prolonging medications (multiple antidepressants, antipsychotics, certain antibiotics/antiarrhythmics, methadone, etc.)
items.risk: QT risk stacking: higher chance of significant QTc prolongation and torsades in susceptible patients.
items.action: Avoid combinations when possible. If combination is necessary, assess risk factors and consider baseline/interval ECG monitoring.

items.with: Anticholinergic medications (tricyclics, benztropine, oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Higher anticholinergic burden: constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision, confusion, delirium, and fall risk—especially in older adults.
items.action: Minimize overlap; choose less anticholinergic alternatives when available.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Hydroxyzine does not have the classic benzodiazepine-style withdrawal or dependence pattern, so most people can stop it without a formal taper. If you’ve been taking it nightly for a long time, you can step down gradually to reduce rebound insomnia or rebound anxiety (which is usually mild and short-lived).
key_points: Most patients: No taper required—stop when no longer needed.
If used nightly for weeks to months: Consider reducing dose or frequency over 1–2 weeks (example: every night → every other night → stop).
Watch for rebound symptoms: temporary insomnia, anxiety, irritability, or daytime grogginess changing as the medication leaves your system.
If symptoms return hard: That’s a signal you need a maintenance strategy (therapy, SSRIs/SNRIs, sleep plan), not more sedation.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Hydroxyzine dosing for psychiatric use is usually PRN (as-needed) and usually kept lower than the absolute maximum because the limiting factor is sedation and next-day impairment.

adult.anxiety_prn: 25–50 mg PO up to 4 times daily as needed; may increase based on response and tolerability up to 100 mg PO 4 times daily (maximum 400 mg/day)
adult.sleep_bedtime: For insomnia associated with anxiety: 25–50 mg PO at bedtime as needed
adult.agitation_prn: 25–50 mg PO as needed for anxiety-related agitation; if IM is used for rapid effect in a monitored setting, 25–50 mg IM as a single dose may be used and can be repeated after 4 hours if needed (IM only)

sections.simple_explanation: This is a sedating antihistamine. The dose that calms anxiety is often the same dose that makes you sleepy—so dosing is a balancing act between relief and functional impairment.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Hydroxyzine is often avoided in pregnancy (especially early pregnancy) and is generally a poor fit for older adults due to anticholinergic side effects and fall risk. Kidney and liver impairment can increase exposure and side effects.
sections.pregnancy: Contraindicated in early pregnancy. Hydroxyzine crosses the placenta. Neonatal withdrawal symptoms (including seizures) have been reported with chronic maternal use or large doses near term. If anxiety treatment is needed in pregnancy, clinicians usually prioritize psychotherapy and medications with better pregnancy safety data.
sections.lactation: It’s not confirmed whether hydroxyzine is present in breast milk. Drowsiness and irritability have been reported in breastfed infants exposed to antihistamines, and sedation has been reported with hydroxyzine exposure. If a first-generation antihistamine is used while breastfeeding, monitor the infant for sedation or irritability. Second-generation antihistamines are generally preferred when an antihistamine is needed.
sections.pediatrics: Not a preferred treatment for pediatric anxiety disorders in modern expert guidance, even though dosing exists. If used, the decision should be cautious and individualized, with a strong bias toward psychotherapy-first strategies.
sections.geriatrics: Avoid use in adults ≥65 when possible. Hydroxyzine has strong anticholinergic effects and can increase confusion, constipation, urinary retention, delirium, and fall risk. Reduced clearance with age can amplify sedation and next-day impairment.
sections.hepatic: In cirrhosis or significant liver impairment: Use the minimum effective dose; do not exceed a total maximum daily dose of 25 mg/day. Use with extra caution if there is any concern for hepatic encephalopathy; discontinue if encephalopathy worsens.
sections.renal: Because the active metabolite (cetirizine) is renally cleared, reduce dosing in kidney impairment. Practical approach: CrCl ≥50 mL/min: no adjustment; CrCl 10 to <50 mL/min: ~50% of usual dose; CrCl <10 mL/min: ~25% to 50% of usual dose. In dialysis contexts, it is unlikely to be significantly dialyzed; dose reductions (25% to 50% of usual dose) are commonly used.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Symptom response: Is anxiety intensity decreasing? Is sleep improving without next-day impairment?
Sedation and functional safety: next-day grogginess, driving impairment, falls risk, work/school performance.
Mental status: confusion, delirium, hallucinations (especially in older adults or with medication stacking).
Anticholinergic side effects: dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision—watch the total anticholinergic burden.

Cardiac risk (QT): assess history of prolonged QT, fainting, palpitations, family history of sudden cardiac death; consider ECG monitoring in high-risk patients or when combined with other QT-prolonging meds.
Electrolytes and medical risk factors when QT risk is relevant: hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, kidney impairment, liver impairment, bradycardia, structural heart disease.
Hypersensitivity or rash: monitor for new or worsening skin reactions; stop and evaluate for severe reactions if concerning rash develops.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Hydroxyzine comes in oral and IM forms. For psychiatric use, it’s most commonly taken by mouth. IM is IM-only and should be used carefully due to route-specific risks.
items: Oral tablets (hydroxyzine HCl): 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg
Oral capsules (hydroxyzine pamoate): 25 mg, 50 mg, 100 mg (Vistaril branded capsules are discontinued in some markets)
IM solution (hydroxyzine HCl): 25 mg/mL and 50 mg/mL (IM only)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Hydroxyzine blocks histamine-1 (H1) receptors in the brain and body. In the brain, that H1 blockade is strongly sedating—which is a big part of why it can feel calming. It also has activity at muscarinic, serotonergic (5-HT2), and dopaminergic receptors, which may contribute to its anxiolytic effect in some people.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Hydroxyzine is best viewed as a short-term, symptom-focused tool: a PRN alternative when you want to avoid benzodiazepines, or a bedtime helper when anxiety is blocking sleep. It’s not a first-line long-term treatment for anxiety disorders. If you find yourself needing it daily for months, that’s usually a sign to build a maintenance plan (therapy, SSRIs/SNRIs, skill-based anxiety treatment, and a real sleep strategy). The two main reasons clinicians avoid it are (1) sedation/anticholinergic burden—especially in older adults—and (2) QT-prolongation risk in susceptible patients.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.q: What is hydroxyzine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, hydroxyzine is most commonly used as a short-term or as-needed option for anxiety symptoms, bedtime anxiety insomnia, or mild anxiety-related agitation. It’s not a long-term maintenance medication for anxiety disorders, but it can be a helpful bridge while therapy or antidepressants start working.

faqs.q: How fast does hydroxyzine work for anxiety?
faqs.a: By mouth, many people feel an effect within 15–30 minutes. Peak effects often show up around 2 hours, which is also when sedation can hit hardest.

Hydroxyzine has a relatively long half-life in adults (around 20 hours on average), so the calming/sedating effect can linger—especially the next morning after a bedtime dose. Older adults and people with liver impairment can feel it longer.

Hydroxyzine is not a benzodiazepine and it does not have the same dependence and withdrawal pattern that makes meds like Xanax risky. That said, it can still be habit-forming in a different way if you use it nightly as your only sleep strategy—because you start relying on sedation instead of building a long-term plan.

faqs.q: Can I take hydroxyzine for sleep?
faqs.a: Yes—when anxiety is the reason you can’t fall asleep, hydroxyzine is sometimes used at bedtime. A common bedtime range is 25–50 mg as needed. The downside is next-day grogginess, so it’s a ‘helpful sometimes’ tool, not a forever solution.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol with hydroxyzine?
faqs.a: No. Alcohol and hydroxyzine both depress the central nervous system. Combining them can cause excessive sedation, poor coordination, blackouts, and dangerous impairment. If you’re using hydroxyzine, skip alcohol.

faqs.q: What’s the QT warning with hydroxyzine?
faqs.a: Hydroxyzine has a conditional risk of QT prolongation (a heart rhythm risk). The danger is higher if you already have a prolonged QT, have electrolyte issues (low potassium or magnesium), have kidney/liver impairment, have bradycardia, have structural heart disease, or take other QT-prolonging medications.

People with prolonged QT should avoid it. Older adults (65+) are usually better off avoiding it because of anticholinergic side effects (confusion, constipation, urinary retention) and fall risk. It’s also generally avoided in early pregnancy.

faqs.q: Is hydroxyzine safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Hydroxyzine is contraindicated in early pregnancy and can cross the placenta. Neonatal withdrawal symptoms have been reported after chronic maternal use or large doses near term. For breastfeeding, it’s not confirmed whether it enters milk, but sedation and irritability have been reported in infants exposed to antihistamines; if used, infants should be monitored, and second-generation antihistamines are generally preferred when an antihistamine is needed.

faqs.q: What’s a typical PRN dose for anxiety?
faqs.a: A common PRN range is 25–50 mg by mouth up to 4 times per day as needed. Some regimens increase based on response and tolerability up to 100 mg four times daily (maximum 400 mg/day), but higher dosing increases sedation and safety risks.
